To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

we develop a framework for deriving lower bounds on the problem kernel size for parameterized problems, we show that the problem kernel size of planar vertex cover, planar independent set, and planar dominating is at least 2k, 4k/5, and 4k/7 respectively unless $\mathcal P$=$\mathcal NP$, and we improve the upper bound for planar dominating from 335k to 67k.
we developed techniques to derive lower and upper bounds on the kernelization complexity of certain problems.

In summary, our research is concerned with
the following questions: What is a problem kernel for a parameterized problem, and how can we find it?
the following question: What is the minimum possible kernel size for a problem parameterized by a certain parameter?
the following questions: (1) How small is the problem kernel for a problem with a given parameter?
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the kernel size for planar dominating is 2^O(sqrt(k)) (Alber et al. 2005), and 4k/5 (our paper) for the other planar problems.
the kernel size of planar dominating set is between 2k and 67k.
planar dominating set has a problem kernel of linear size.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
for many problems we can show lower bounds on the problem kernel, and for the remaining problems we can show improved upper bounds on the problem kernels.
for a wide range of parameterized problems on planar graphs we have either lower bounds or upper bounds on the problem kernel, and for some problems we even have both.

we develop a new technique to derive kernel lower bounds and use this technique to derive lower bounds for planar vertex cover, planar independent set, planar dominating set and planar feedback vertex set.
The main takeaway from our work is that
we develop a general technique to derive lower and upper bounds on kernel size for a large class of problems, and we show how to apply this technique to several problems.
the techniques developed for deriving kernel upper bounds can be used to derive kernel lower bounds, thus making kernelization more of a two-sided problem.
the kernelization lower bound techniques of Bodlaender et al. can be used in conjunction with the parametric duality framework of Marx to obtain new kernel lower bounds.
